aquinas-virtues: In the ethics of Thomas Aquinas, human excellence is organized around two sets of virtues. The four cardinal virtues—prudence, justice, fortitude, and temperance—are acquired through habit and reason and were inherited from classical antiquity, governing how a person deliberates and acts well in ordinary life. The three theological virtues—faith, hope, and charity—are, by contrast, held to be infused by grace and to orient the person toward God as the ultimate end. Together they express Aquinas's synthesis of Aristotelian moral psychology with Christian theology, in which natural virtue is completed rather than replaced by the supernatural.
ockham-razor: Ockham's Razor is the methodological principle that, among competing explanations, one should not multiply entities or assumptions beyond necessity, so that the simpler account is to be preferred when it explains the evidence equally well. Named for the fourteenth-century logician William of Ockham, who favored parsimony in his rejection of superfluous metaphysical posits, it functions as a rule of theoretical economy rather than a proof of truth. It responds to the temptation to explain phenomena by inventing unobserved causes, urging that explanatory machinery be justified by what it actually accounts for.
avicenna-floating-man: The Floating Man is a thought experiment devised by the Persian philosopher Avicenna to show that self-awareness does not depend on the body or the senses. He asks us to imagine a person created fully formed but suspended in empty space, blindfolded and touching nothing, so that no sensory information reaches them; even in this condition, Avicenna argues, the person would still affirm their own existence. From this he concludes that the soul knows itself immediately and is distinct from the body, an argument sometimes seen as a distant forerunner of Descartes's cogito.
averroes-reason-revelation: The Concord of Reason and Revelation is the position, developed by the Andalusian philosopher Averroes, that philosophical demonstration and religious scripture cannot ultimately conflict because both issue from the same truth. Where a literal reading of scripture appears to contradict what reason establishes, Averroes held that the text should be interpreted allegorically, since the two are simply different routes to a single reality. Responding to theologians who attacked philosophy as impious, he argued that rational inquiry is not only permitted but obligatory for those capable of it, and that religion addresses different audiences through different modes of speech.
descartes-cogito: The Cogito is René Descartes's claim, captured in the phrase 'I think, therefore I am,' that the very act of doubting or thinking guarantees the existence of the thinker. Seeking an indubitable foundation for knowledge, Descartes found that while he could doubt the external world and even his own body, he could not coherently doubt that he was doing the doubting. The Cogito thus serves as the first certainty on which he attempts to rebuild a secure system of knowledge, and it places the self-conscious subject at the center of modern epistemology.
cartesian-doubt: Methodological doubt is the procedure by which René Descartes deliberately suspended belief in everything that could possibly be false, in order to find whatever might survive as certain. He pushed this doubt to its extreme by imagining an all-powerful evil demon bent on deceiving him about mathematics, the senses, and the external world, so that no ordinary belief could be trusted uncritically. The exercise is not skepticism for its own sake but a purifying method: by discarding all that is dubitable, Descartes aims to isolate a foundation, the thinking self, secure enough to ground the rest of knowledge.
cartesian-dualism: Mind–body dualism is René Descartes's view that reality contains two fundamentally different kinds of substance: mind, whose essence is thought and which is non-extended, and body, whose essence is extension in space. On this account a human being is a union of an immaterial thinking soul and a material, mechanical body, each intelligible without the other. The position sharpens the enduring problem of how two such distinct substances can causally interact, and it set much of the agenda for later philosophy of mind, which has largely wrestled with the difficulties it bequeathed.
spinoza-monism: Substance monism is Baruch Spinoza's doctrine that there exists only one infinite substance, which he identifies with God and nature alike in the phrase Deus sive Natura, 'God or Nature.' Everything that exists—minds, bodies, and events—is not a separate thing but a mode or modification of this single substance, expressed through its infinite attributes, of which we grasp thought and extension. Rejecting the idea of a transcendent creator standing apart from the world, Spinoza reconceives God as the immanent, necessary system of reality itself, from which all things follow.
spinoza-conatus: Conatus is Baruch Spinoza's term for the striving by which each thing endeavors to persevere in its own being. In his Ethics this striving is not an added desire but the very essence of a thing: to exist is to resist dissolution and to maintain oneself. In human beings the conatus appears as the drive toward self-preservation and flourishing, and Spinoza uses it to ground his account of emotion and value, explaining desire, joy, and sorrow as functions of whether one's power of acting is increased or diminished.
spinoza-determinism: Spinozist necessity is the claim that everything that happens follows with strict necessity from the nature of the one substance, so that nothing in the universe could have been otherwise. Because God or Nature acts solely from the necessity of its own essence, there is no free will in the sense of an uncaused choice, and even human decisions are fully determined by prior causes. Spinoza does not treat this as bleak fatalism but as the basis of freedom rightly understood: liberation comes through understanding the causes that determine us, replacing passive bondage to the passions with active knowledge.
best-possible-world: The doctrine of the best of all possible worlds is Gottfried Leibniz's answer to the problem of evil, holding that a perfectly wise and good God, surveying every possible world, necessarily chose to create the one with the greatest overall balance of goodness. Apparent evils and imperfections are permitted only because they are inseparable from a greater good or a richer, more harmonious whole. Since God could not do less than the best, the actual world, for all its flaws, must be optimal—a claim Voltaire later famously satirized but which Leibniz meant as a serious defense of divine justice.
monadology: Monadology is Gottfried Leibniz's metaphysics of simple, indivisible, immaterial substances he called monads, which are the true elements of reality. Each monad is a self-contained point of perception with no windows, meaning it does not causally interact with others; instead their states are coordinated by a divinely established pre-established harmony so that the whole universe is mirrored, from its own perspective, within each one. On this view the material world of extended bodies is a well-founded appearance grounded in these mind-like unities rather than in inert matter.
sufficient-reason: The Principle of Sufficient Reason, central to Gottfried Leibniz's philosophy, states that nothing is the case, and nothing happens, without a reason why it is so rather than otherwise. Paired with the principle of non-contradiction, it governs all truths of fact and drives Leibniz's arguments in metaphysics, including his cases for God's existence and for the best possible world. It expresses a deep confidence that reality is thoroughly intelligible: every fact, however contingent, is in principle explicable, and there are no brute, reasonless features of the world.
pascals-wager: Pascal's Wager is Blaise Pascal's argument that belief in God is the rational bet even under uncertainty about whether God exists. Reasoning that the matter cannot be settled by proof, Pascal frames it as a decision under risk: if one believes and God exists, the gain is infinite, while if God does not exist, the loss is slight; disbelief risks an infinite loss for a small worldly gain. Because an infinite potential reward outweighs any finite stake, he concludes that prudence favors wagering on faith, a move often regarded as an early piece of decision theory as much as theology.
montaigne-skepticism: Que sais-je?—'What do I know?'—is the motto that captures Michel de Montaigne's tempered skepticism, an attitude of habitual questioning rather than dogmatic denial. Writing in the sixteenth century, Montaigne doubted the reach of human reason and the reliability of the senses, noting how custom, perspective, and mood shape what people take to be certain. Rather than despairing, he turned this doubt into a mode of self-examination in his Essays, using suspended judgment as a way to live modestly, tolerantly, and attentively to the shifting realities of experience.
